plan.contextChunk: This figure is a compact three-dimensional vector diagram drawn on a set of coordinate axes. The z-axis rises vertically, the y-axis extends to the right, and the x-axis runs toward the lower left, out of the page; all three are thin black lines with small arrowheads and italic labels, meeting at an unlabeled origin. Two purple dots mark positions in space, P_1 sitting above and to the right of the origin and P_2 lower and farther to the right. A thick purple arrow from the origin to P_1 is labeled r(t_1) and a second purple arrow from the origin to P_2 is labeled r(t_2), both symbols carrying overhead vector arrows. A third purple arrow of the same weight runs directly from P_1 to P_2 and is labeled delta r. The three arrows close into a triangle, so the picture shows the displacement as exactly the vector that must be added to the earlier position vector to arrive at the later one. Casting the difference of two position vectors as a single arrow drawn between the two points extends the one-dimensional idea of displacement to motion anywhere in space.

elements: thin black x-axis starting at the origin and projecting diagonally down-left with an arrowhead and italic label x near its tip
thin black y-axis starting at the origin and projecting horizontally to the right with an arrowhead and italic label y near its tip
thin black z-axis starting at the origin and projecting vertically upward with an arrowhead and italic label z near its tip
unlabeled origin where the three coordinate axes meet
purple position point P1 above and to the right of the origin
purple position point P2 lower and farther to the right than P1
thick purple arrow vector r(t1) from the origin to P1
thick purple arrow vector r(t2) from the origin to P2
thick purple displacement arrow vector delta r from P1 to P2
label P1 next to the upper purple point
label P2 next to the lower-right purple point
label vector r(t1) placed near the origin-to-P1 arrow
label vector r(t2) placed near the origin-to-P2 arrow
label delta vector Delta r placed beside the P1-to-P2 arrow

interactions.teaches: Moving either position point changes both position vectors and the displacement vector, making clear that displacement is the vector difference between final and initial positions

interactions.label: Build the displacement
interactions.teaches: The displacement vector is not another origin-based position vector; it is the change that carries the earlier position P1 to the later position P2

demo_steps.title: Initial position vector
demo_steps.narration: First show only r(t1), the position vector from the origin to the earlier point P1. This establishes P1 as a location measured from the coordinate origin.

demo_steps.title: Final position vector
demo_steps.narration: Add r(t2), the position vector from the origin to the later point P2. Both locations are now described relative to the same origin.

demo_steps.title: Displacement
demo_steps.narration: Add Delta r from P1 to P2. The triangle closes, showing that r(t1) plus Delta r equals r(t2), so Delta r = r(t2) - r(t1).

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a compact axonometric 3D vector diagram. World axes should project visually as in the source: +Z vertical upward, +Y nearly horizontal to the right, and +X diagonally down-left out of the page. Axis lengths: z about 2.8 units, y about 3.1 units, x about 1.7 units; all meet at origin (0,0,0). Initial point coordinates should place the vectors nearly in the yz plane: P1 approximately (0, 1.65, 1.55), P2 approximately (0, 2.65, -0.45). Thus r(t1)=P1-origin, r(t2)=P2-origin, and Delta r=P2-P1. Draw P1 above/right of origin and P2 lower/farther right; the displacement arrow slopes steeply down-right from P1 to P2. Axes are black #111111, thin strokes. Vectors and points are purple/magenta #8a1f86 or #8e248c, with vector strokes about 3-4 times the axis thickness. Points are small filled spheres or disks, radius about 0.07-0.09 world units. Labels are black, italic math style where possible: x, y, z, P_1, P_2, vector r(t_1), vector r(t_2), and Delta vector r. Label placement: r(t1) just below/along the upper origin-to-P1 arrow, r(t2) below the lower origin-to-P2 arrow, Delta r to the right of the P1-to-P2 arrow, P1 just above/right of the upper point, P2 just below/right of the lower point.
interactionPlan.notes: Implement vectors as cylinder/shaft plus cone arrowheads or thick Line2 segments with cone tips. Endpoint dragging should constrain to a visible 3D drag plane by default but allow modifier-key depth adjustment if supported; update all dependent arrows and labels continuously. Keep the triangle exactly closed by computing Delta r from the current P1 and P2 positions rather than storing it independently. In sequence states, show vectors cumulatively: showR1 displays only r(t1); showR1AndR2 displays r(t1) and r(t2); showAll displays all three vectors and both point labels.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Drag point P1 or P2: learner moves either endpoint in 3D space; r(t1), r(t2), and delta r redraw immediately while the triangle relation closes; the vector difference delta r = r(t2) - r(t1) becomes visible as the arrow between positions.
- Button sequence from initial position to final position: learner steps from origin-to-P1, then origin-to-P2, then P1-to-P2; each vector appears in order; the displacement is understood as the change needed to carry the earlier position vector to the later one.

authoredContext:
With our definition of the position of a particle in three-dimensional space, we can formulate the three-dimensional displacement. The figure shows a particle at time t1 located at P1 with position vector r→(t1). At a later time t2, the particle is located at P2 with position vector r→(t2). The displacement vector Δr→ is found by subtracting r→(t1) from r→(t2):

Vector addition is discussed in Vectors. Note that this is the same operation we did in one dimension, but now the vectors are in three-dimensional space.

The displacement Δr→=r→(t2)−r→(t1) is the vector from P1 to P2.

An x y z coordinate system is shown, with positive x out of the page, positive y to the right, and positive z up. Two points, P 1 and P 2 are shown. The vector r of t 1 from the origin to P 1 and the vector r of t 2 from the origin to P 2 are shown as purple arrows. The vector delta r is shown as a purple arrow whose tail is at P 1 and head at P 2.

The following examples illustrate the concept of displacement in multiple dimensions.

discrepancies: The vector labels render with a placeholder square/tofu after r in the screenshot instead of a clean vector arrow notation, especially for r(t2) and Δr.
Purple arrowheads and endpoint spheres are much bulkier than the small arrows/dots in the source and partially obscure the endpoints.
The generated figure is more zoomed out with a side control panel, making the textbook diagram occupy less of the visual area than the compact source figure.
evaluation.notes: The generated diagram captures the displacement-vector geometry well, but the vector notation labels render poorly and the arrow/point styling is too heavy compared with the source.
action_items: Replace combining vector-arrow label markup with robust HTML such as bold italic r plus a separate arrow, or use plain \u2192 notation to avoid square placeholder glyphs.
Reduce the purple arrowhead sizes and endpoint sphere radii to better match the source figure's thinner arrows and small point markers.
Increase the default zoom or framing so the axis-vector diagram fills the available canvas more like the reference.
